sections.html:
Fredericksburg is a compact independent city of roughly 10.5 square miles on the Rappahannock River, about 53 miles south of downtown Washington, D.C. Stafford County lies across the water to the north and east, and Spotsylvania County wraps the south and west. It stands on the fall line, at about 59 feet of elevation. Interstate 95, U.S. 1 and U.S. 17 all pass through, and Route 3 heads west toward the big shopping centers and on to Culpeper.

The Census Bureau counted 27,982 residents in 2020 and estimates 30,393 for 2025. The city became independent in 1879, so no county sits between it and the state. It bills its own real estate tax, and a house just over a boundary street in Spotsylvania or Stafford is taxed by a different government.

sections.h2: Older houses and the Historic District
sections.html:
Founded in 1728 as a colonial port at the farthest point boats could travel up the Rappahannock, Fredericksburg later stood midway between the Union and Confederate capitals and saw the Battle of Fredericksburg in 1862. The 40-block Fredericksburg Historic District, listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1971, holds more than 350 buildings from the 18th and 19th centuries.

Houses in or near the district are often old, and old houses tend to bring slate or tin roofs, plaster walls, stone foundations and wiring older than modern code. The Commissioner of the Revenue lists a rehab tax credit for improving residential property in the Historic District. The real estate section at 540-372-1207 explains who qualifies.

The University of Mary Washington, Mary Washington Healthcare and GEICO are the major employers, and tourism adds to the mix, with about 1.5 million visitors a year to the battlefield park, museums and downtown. Germanna Community College also has a campus here.

Many residents commute by car, bus and rail to Washington, Richmond, and Fairfax, Prince William and Arlington counties. Most of the traffic heads north at peak hours on I-95 and U.S. 1, and the Route 1 bridge over the Rappahannock is often a bottleneck. The Virginia Railway Express and Amtrak serve commuters, and the FRED bus covers most of the area.

A landlord with a worn-out rental near the university or a commuter route sometimes decides to sell rather than renovate. A buyer tied to a Washington commute weighs the drive heavily, so a seller on a short timeline cannot count on that buyer arriving soon.

Summers are hot and humid and winters cool. The average July high is 88.5 degrees, the average January low 25.1, and about 43.4 inches of precipitation fall in a year. Humidity feeds mold in basements and crawl spaces, winter freezes test pipes and masonry, and an older roof can fail after a run of hot summers and wet storms.

  • Inspect the roof, gutters and flashing before listing.
  • Look for dampness along the foundation and in the lower walls.
  • Check older heating and cooling equipment, since failures tend to arrive at the worst time.

Fredericksburg bills real estate tax twice a year, with payments due December 5 and June 5. Real estate is reassessed every four years, and billing follows a fiscal year that runs from July 1 through June 30.

Tax detailAmount or date
Real estate rate, fiscal year ended June 30, 2026$0.80 per $100 of assessed value
Fire tax, started July 1, 2024$0.01 per $100 of valuation
First-half bill (July to December)Due December 5
Second-half bill (January to June)Due June 5
Penalty on unpaid balances10 percent after each due date

Call the real estate office for the rate now in effect. It is at 715 Princess Anne Street, Room 107, phone 540-372-1207. The Treasurer notes that supplemental real estate bills can arrive on other dates in some cases.

At settlement, the closing agent pays any real estate tax that is due, and Virginia's grantor tax is collected on the deed. A tax lien here sits ahead of every other lien and stays until the city receives payment. Your contract spells out how the year's tax is shared between you and the buyer.

The grantor tax equals 50 cents on each $500 of price, and unless the contract says otherwise the seller bears it. The clerk of court takes the money when the deed is recorded, and the first page of the deed must state the consideration.

  • Get the balance owed on the December 5 or June 5 installment from the Treasurer.
  • Find out whether the 10 percent penalty has been added yet.
  • Ask the title company for a lien search before you sign anything.
  • Write into the contract how the half-year tax is divided.

A bill that has gone unpaid for a while grows through the penalty, so settle it or have it paid from proceeds at closing rather than letting it ride.

Owners here frequently hold an older house, a rental or an inherited property, and many of them live far away. Historic-age houses may need repairs a lender would insist on, and a house near I-95 or Route 1 can have noise issues that buyers push on. Reagan National and Dulles lie to the north and Richmond International to the south, but rush-hour traffic runs north.

Selling for cash removes repair demands, showings and loan approval from the picture. Some deals we close ourselves and some go to a vetted cash buyer, and either way the offer reflects the house's condition and title. Weigh it against listing and against a local investor's bid.

sections.h2: How the process runs, start to finish
sections.html:
Begin by telling us about the house and whether a tenant lives in it. We review photos or visit, then hand you a written offer. Accept it, and a title company searches the records and prepares the deed, any payoff letters and the settlement statement.

Collect the deed, the latest tax bill, loan payoff details, the lease if it is a rental and, for an inherited house, papers that show who may sign. The closing date is yours to pick within what the title work allows. A tenant can remain in the house, and the lease carries over after the sale.

Before you accept, put numbers on the alternative. Repairs a lender would require, agent fees and months of tax, utilities and insurance can add up on an old house. Compare that net with the cash offer, and ask any buyer to state who pays for title work.

faqs.q: When are Fredericksburg real estate taxes due?
faqs.a: Real estate tax is due December 5 and June 5, or the next business day. The city adds a 10 percent penalty to balances left unpaid after those dates.

faqs.q: What is the real estate tax rate in Fredericksburg, VA?
faqs.a: For the fiscal year that ended June 30, 2026, the city listed $0.80 per $100 of assessed value, plus a fire tax of $0.01 per $100. Call 540-372-1207 for the rate now in effect.

faqs.q: How often does Fredericksburg reassess real estate?
faqs.a: Real estate is reassessed every four years. Call the Commissioner of the Revenue at 540-372-1207 with questions about your assessment.

faqs.q: Is there a tax credit for fixing up a house in the Fredericksburg Historic District?
faqs.a: The city lists a rehab tax credit for improving residential property in the Historic District. Contact the Commissioner of the Revenue's real estate section at 540-372-1207 to learn who qualifies.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Fredericksburg rental or inherited house as-is?
faqs.a: Yes. A cash buyer can purchase it in its current condition, with a tenant in place if needed. The title company still handles payoffs and the deed.
